title: quantization-sanity-sweep-aug2025
content:
Purpose:
Quick internal sweep to compare practical perf/quality tradeoffs across INT8 (dynamic/static), FP8 emulation, GPTQ (4-bit/8-bit variants), and AWQ on two representative models. Goal: identify which quant modes we can safely recommend for hosted/dedicated tiers, and which kernel hotspots need engineering work. Draft notes, rough numbers, follow-up tasks.

Summary (TL;DR):
- INT8 (dynamic per-channel) with fused GEMM kernels delivers the best latency/throughput win with minimal quality drop (~0.5-1.5% EM on our QA set) on 7B/13B class models.
- GPTQ (4-bit) reduces memory ~2-3x vs FP16 and often preserves top-1 generation quality for short prompts, but degrades on long-context or heavy reasoning prompts (3-8% EM drop).
- AWQ 4-bit tends to be slightly better than baseline GPTQ on our subjective evals, but is more sensitive to kernel precision (needs specialized matmul kernels).
- FP8 (emulated) shows promising model-size reduction and slightly improved latency in kernels that support 8-bit float math, but ecosystem/kernel support is inconsistent - fails gracefully but spotty speedups.

Experimental setup:
- Hardware: A100-40GB (PCIe) and H100-80GB (early access cluster). Most numbers below are A100 unless noted.
- Models: llama2-13b-chat (v2.0) quantized variants, vicuna-7b-v1.5, and a curated redwood-mini-eval-50 (QA+code-gen+open-ended) prompt set.
- Runtime: rw-serving v2.7.3 (local branch quant-bench), Triton v23.11, CUDA 12.1, cuBLASLt + custom fused GEMM.
- Quant libraries tested: bitsandbytes(0.40), GPTQ-for-LLaMa (fork), AWQ (latest commit as of 2025-08-01), FP8 emulation shim (internal).
- Metrics collected: p50/p95 token latency (ms), tokens/sec, GPU memory (peak), CPU overhead (sys%), and quality: exact-match (EM) on QA subset, token logprob delta relative to FP16 baseline, and subjective spot-check for hallucination.
- Profiling: Nsight Systems (frames), nvprof traces for matmul kernels, Triton metrics for batch aggregation, and lightweight wall-clock tracing instrumented in runtime.

Representative command lines (how to reproduce locally):
- baseline (FP16): rw-infer --model llama2-13b --dtype fp16 --batch 1 --seq 512 --profile out/fp16.trace
- int8 dynamic + fused kernel: rw-infer --model llama2-13b --quant int8_dynamic --kernel fused-gemm --batch 1 --seq 512 --profile out/int8dyn.trace
- gptq 4-bit: rw-infer --model llama2-13b-gptq-4bit --quant gptq --kernel gptq-kernel --batch 1 --seq 512 --profile out/gptq4.trace
- awq 4-bit: rw-infer --model llama2-13b-awq-4bit --quant awq --kernel awq-triton --batch 1 --seq 512 --profile out/awq4.trace
- fp8 emu: rw-infer --model llama2-13b --dtype fp8_emulated --kernel fp8-fused --batch 1 --seq 512 --profile out/fp8.trace

Key perf numbers (median of 10 runs, A100-40GB, seq=512, batch=1, single-token sampling):
- FP16 baseline (fused-gemm): p50=38ms, p95=58ms, tokens/sec=26, GPU mem=22.1GB
- INT8 dynamic (fused-gemm): p50=26ms, p95=41ms, tokens/sec=38, GPU mem=12.8GB (peak)
- GPTQ 4-bit (gptq-kernel): p50=22ms, p95=46ms, tokens/sec=44, GPU mem=9.2GB
- AWQ 4-bit (awq-triton): p50=20ms, p95=40ms, tokens/sec=48, GPU mem=8.8GB
- FP8 emulated (fp8-fused): p50=33ms, p95=55ms, tokens/sec=30, GPU mem=13.5GB

Quality (redwood-mini-eval-50, relative EM to FP16 baseline=100%):
- FP16 baseline: EM=100 (reference)
- INT8 dynamic: EM=97-99 (median 98.2) - degradation concentrated on low-frequency factual queries and math tasks.
- GPTQ 4-bit: EM=93-97 (median 95.4) - stable on short-span retrieval but worse on multi-step reasoning.
- AWQ 4-bit: EM=94-96 (median 95.8) - slightly better subjective fluency vs GPTQ in our spot-check.
- FP8 emulated: EM=99-100 (median 99.3) - quality very close to FP16 on this eval set.

Profiling highlights / bottlenecks observed:
- Matmul dominates runtime in all quant modes (40-65% of GPU op time). However the kernel type matters: fused GEMM (fused transpose+GEMM) reduces memory traffic and improves INT8 latency significantly.
- KV cache writes/reads are a nontrivial overhead for long contexts - observed 8-12% overhead increase when seq>1024, especially for formats that require unpack/repacks for quantized KV.
- Dequant/quantization casting steps are visible in nvprof traces for INT8-inferred layers that still do some FP32 accumulation - need fusion with matmul for best perf.
- Attention softmax and rotary embedding ops are sensitive to FP precision; FP8 emulation caused occasional FP saturation effects requiring small learning-rate style corrections in calibration (we used calibration tables).
- AWQ/GPTQ kernels suffer from reduced occupancy on older A100 driver stacks; on H100 the occupancy and warp utilization improved and p50 dropped another ~8-12% for those kernels.

Notes on kernels and engineering implications:
- Fused GEMM (our custom kernel) + int8 dynamic is the lowest friction win for hosted API: small code surface, consistent perf, and acceptable quality drop. Prioritize hardening these kernels across our runtime backends.
- GPTQ kernels need more attention: implement a fused dequant+matmul path to avoid expensive per-tensor conversions during inference. Also re-evaluate packing strategy for cache-friendly layout.
- AWQ shows promise but is fragile without optimized kernels for matmul and attention; consider upstreaming selective kernels to Triton for cross-platform usage.
- FP8: if we invest in an FP8 path with mixed-precision accumulation (FP32 accum), we can achieve near-FP16 quality with sustained perf wins, but vendor and library support (cuBLAS/oneAPI) is still catching up.

Observed failure modes / gotchas during runs:
- Some GPTQ-converted weights from third-party scripts had unexpected quantization bias - seen as consistent logits shift; fixed by re-centering zero-point during conversion.
- AWQ models occasionally cause non-deterministic generation on repeat runs due to different rounding strategies in CPU calibration step. Need to lock calibration RNG seeds and add a sanity-check.
- FP8 emulation on A100 with older CUDA drivers produced NaNs in a small subset of attention heads; upgrading CUDA to 12.1 avoided this.

Recommendations (short-term):
1) For hosted tier fast-follow: enable INT8 dynamic with fused-gemm kernel as opt-in beta. Provide a compatibility guardrail (EM drop detection via eval prompt set).
2) Invest 2-3 sprints to fuse GPTQ dequant+matmul path and re-benchmark; aim to match AWQ latency with GPTQ quality.
3) Prototype FP8 path on H100-only pool for Dedicated customers that opt-in; monitor NaN/regression risk and build calibration pipeline.
4) Add KV caching format tests for quantized weights to avoid expensive re-packing on long-context requests.

Next experiments (medium-term):
- Run 1k-prompt long-context sweep (seq 4096) to measure KV overheads across quant modes.
- A/B deploy INT8 dynamic in US-hosted-small pool for 2 weeks on low-traffic models; track cost delta and regen-quality alerts.
- End-to-end latency profiling including network + batcher for batch sizes 1-16 to see real customer impact.

Open questions / TBD:
- What is acceptable EM/LLR (loglike ratio) drop for our SLAs in hosted vs dedicated customers? Define thresholds per customer tier.
- Should we expose multiple quant modes in API or hide behind service-side model variants? (UX + support cost tradeoff).
- How much engineering cost to add FP8-safe kernels vs incremental GPTQ improvements? Prioritization request to infra/product.

Appendix (quick artifacts):
- redwood-mini-eval-50 sample prompts: ["wiki-fact: When was the Eiffel Tower completed?","math: 15*23", "code: sort list in python", "multi-hop: summarize X then infer Y"]
- Example nvprof snippet (matmul hotspot): kernel=cublasLt_matmul  avg_time=1.8ms  calls=1345  bytes=XXGB
- Conversion checklist for GPTQ/AWQ weights: 1) validate zero-point 2) run small synthetic forward 3) compare logits to FP16 on 10 seeds 4) run redwood-mini-eval-50 sanity

Notes to reviewers: this is a working sweep, numbers are noisy (10-run medians). Please comment inline if you have conversions/benchmarks to add (esp. H100 numbers). Prioritize reproducibility: I put commands above.
